newsitem.title: USA: Study says name-brand, generic thyroid drugs equal.
newsitem.headline: Study says name-brand, generic thyroid drugs equal.

text.p: Four brand-name and generic drugs for treating hypothyroidism were found to be equally effective in a disputed 1990 study published Tuesday in the Journal of the American Medical Association.
But the maker of one of the brand-name drugs said the study was flawed and said there were inaccuracies in a Journal editorial accompanying the study.

The seven-year-old study showed equivalence among four hypothyroidism treatments -- the name-brand drugs Synthroid and Levoxyl, and two generic products -- all versions from different manufacturers of levothyroxine sodium. The medicine is taken for life by hypothyroidism sufferers, who number about eight million in the United States.

"Based on our findings, we believe that the four generic and brand-name preparations in this study are bioequivalent by current (U.S.) Food and Drug Administration criteria for oral drugs and are interchangeable without loss of therapeutic efficacy in the majority of patients for treatment of hypothyroidism," concluded Dr. Betty Dong and colleagues at the University of California Medical Centre in San Francisco.
The university researchers called for further study to determine whether all levothyroxine sodium medications, not just the four they looked at, are equal.
"Demonstration of bioequivalence between brand-name and generic preparations should enhance cost-effectiveness for patients receiving lifelong thyroxine replacement therapy," the researchers said.
The Dong study involved 22 women with hypothyroidism and was supported in part by a grant from Boots Pharmaceutical Inc, the manufacturer of Synthroid, the journal said.

The Dong study was largely completed in 1990, but has been the subject of a dispute ever since between the researchers and their sponsors, according to an unusual journal editorial accompanying the publication of the study.

In the editorial, journal deputy editor and University of California-San Francisco researcher Dr. Drummond Rennie wrote that Boots Pharmaceutical tried for years to suppress and discredit the Dong study.
"Boots waged an energetic campaign to discredit the study and prevent publication of the drafts Dong and her colleagues sent to them for comment, claiming that the study was flawed," Rennie wrote.

The dispute involved university officials and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration before Boots agreed in November 1996 not to block publication of the manuscript, Rennie wrote. Boots was purchased purchased in 1995 by the Knoll Pharmaceutical unit of Germany's BASF AG.
In a statement issued on Tuesday, Knoll (formerly Boots) said it "strongly disagrees with the validity of the (Dong) study."
"The company believes that the study contains major flaws in design and execution, and fails to support the authors' conclusions," Knoll said.

The company said it was "troubled by both the inaccuracies contained in the accompanying JAMA editorial, authored by Dr. Drummond Rennie, and Dr. Rennie's clear conflict of interest as a faculty member at UCSF."
The company said, "The editorial falsely portrays the conduct of the company and its interaction with the study investigators."

Of the other drugs involved in the study, Levoxyl, formerly called Levoxine, was made by Daniels Pharmaceuticals Inc, which was acquired last year by Jones Medical Industries Inc, of St. Louis, Mo. The two generic versions of the drug were made by Pharmaceutical Basics Inc, of Denver, and distributed under the Geneva Generics and Rugby Laboratories labels, according to the journal article.
